articles.title: Americast - Americanswers… on 5 Live! Why is Lindsay Clancy’s mistrial dividing America? - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: And will Trump succeed in limiting mail-in voting before the midterms?
articles.body: And will Trump’s attempts to limit mail-in voting at the US Supreme Court succeed? The US president has made an urgent appeal, trying to change the rules over who can and can’t vote by mail before this November’s midterm elections, despite ballot papers being posted out in several states. In this episode, Sarah, Sumi and Marianna are answering your questions with Matt Chorley from 5 Live. We look at why Lindsay Clancy’s mistrial has become over-run with conspiracy theories, and what is likely to happen next. Clancy has admitted killing her three children, in one of America’s biggest murder trials, widely covered on US television and social media platforms. Plus, what credentials does Trump’s son in law Jared Kushner have when it comes to being a peace envoy, after his meetings with Presidents Zelensky and Putin this weekend? And how seriously should we take Trump’s proposals for a new Space Force uniform, with many people comparing the designs to those worn by Nazi SS officers. articles.title: 11 reasons why Quibi crashed and burned in less than a year
articles.summary: Quibi was a $2 billion bet from Jeffrey Katzenberg and Meg Whitman that shortform video streaming would work. After less than a year of being on the market, the company has shut down. Here are 11 reasons why that happened.
articles.body: Quibi, the shortform video streaming service designed for people to enjoy on their phones, has shuttered after less than a year of existence. Led by veteran Hollywood executive Jeffrey Katzenberg and former HP CEO Meg Whitman, the streaming service was designed to be a revolutionary way to watch videos on the go, with shows and films specifically formatted to work in both landscape and portrait modes. With nearly $2 billion raised before Quibi even launched in April and a long line of Hollywood talent on board to provide movies and shows, Katzenberg and Whitman felt pretty good about their prospects — even if analysts and media critics questioned the duo’s strategy. Then the United States joined the rest of the world in shutting down due to the COVID-19 pandemic just a few weeks before Quibi launched. Quibi, a streaming service built around the premise that people would watch its shows on the go, now faced an entire population of potential subscribers stuck at home. In its brief six months of life, Quibi also faced a lawsuit backed by a wealthy foe, subscriber woes, and product feature hump. It never managed to escape being the app to ridicule. So why did Quibi fail? Those factors all played in, but it was executives’ fatal misunderstanding of what Quibi should be that led to its inevitable and rapid downfall. [Image: Quibi’s Survive, a show about someone doing a thing that the company could not 1. Nearly all of Quibi’s shows were terrible It’s the most obvious reason but also arguably the biggest. An entertainment streaming service needs titles that are going to convince subscribers to sign up and stay, but Quibi was packed with mediocre content that seemed to come from studios and networks happy to finally sell off the projects sitting on their basement floors for years. Katzenberg and Whitman invested more than $1 billion in top Hollywood talent, and projects from top studios, that nevertheless failed to produce anything of quality. Most titles felt like jokes straight out of 30 Rock. Then there were “Daily Essentials,” a lineup of programming that appeared daily and focused on a certain subject, like recapping late night shows or giving sports updates. They were the equivalent to videos found on YouTube — except on YouTube, the same type of content was better and free. (Disclosure: Vox Media is partnered with Quibi on two shows and there were discussions for a Verge show in the future.) There’s a reason I bet 99 percent of people reading this can’t recall more than a few Quibi originals. Wireless? Die Hart? Survive? Do any of these ring a bell? The only show I can remember is Murder Unboxed, and it never even premiered. Nothing about Quibi’s shows were at all memorable. 2. People’s daily lives changed; Quibi didn’t Quibi was designed to be watched on phones, and for the longest time, Quibi executives seemed reluctant to budge on that design. Quibi seemed positively opposed to adapting to its new world at first. The company relented and slowly started adding support for Apple’s AirPlay and Google’s Chromecast so people could cast from their phones, but doing so disabled Quibi’s Turnstyle technology, the only thing really setting its shows apart at this point. It wasn’t an ideal fix. Quibi didn’t actually release an app for Fire TV and Roku set-top boxes until this week… just one day before Katzenberg and Whitman announced they were closing up shop. 3. Quibi failed to invest in the power of memes The only viral Quibi clip was recorded from another phone. Quibi didn’t launch with the ability to take screenshots or share clips from its shows and films, and without those sharing features, there was no way for people to easily discover and engage with Quibi’s series. This all speaks to the company being led by people with no real understanding of what the future of entertainment is, especially on mobile devices: it’s not just about what people are watching, but the interactivity of turning what you’re watching into content across your own social media networks. 4. Quibi’s price was too damn high The fact that Quibi charged $5 a month for garbage bin entertainment (or $8 a month without ads) was nonsensical. The entertainment people were getting for free on platforms like TikTok, YouTube, and Twitch, combined with the highly talked-about shows and movies they were paying for already on Netflix, Amazon, and Disney Plus, left Quibi’s additional price not exactly something to be desired. Quibi tested a completely ad-supported free tier in Australia and New Zealand a couple of months before the company shuttered, but by that point, it was too little, too late. 5. Did anyone outside of Media Twitter know about Quibi? Think back to the last time you saw an ad for Quibi on TV, Instagram, or TikTok. What about a specific show? Quibi was notably bad at marketing. There was an expensive Super Bowl ad that failed to actually demonstrate what Quibi was (that ran months before Quibi was available), leaving people more confused than anything else. None of the ads for shows ever traveled on TikTok, Instagram, Twitter, or Facebook. Arguably, part of the reason Quibi and its various series, including many of its multimillion-dollar bets, never took off is because no one outside of Media Twitter knew they even existed. [Image: 6. Problems at the very top Before Quibi launched, Whitman and Katzenberg were already running into problems with each other. Whitman threatened to quit as the company’s CEO, finding that Katzenberg was dictatorial, undermined her authority, and belittled her, according to The Wall Street Journal. On top of that, neither Katzenberg nor Whitman truly seemed to understand how people use their phones, what people want from streaming services, or why something like TikTok and Netflix worked. It’s hard enough to get a company off the ground in an increasingly competitive market; it’s near impossible if the two heads of that company can barely work together. 7. Why should Quibi exist? Quibi never figured it out The problem that Quibi could never address was, “Why do I need this?” Katzenberg and Whitman repeatedly said “we’re not competing with Netflix,” but Quibi was competing with Netflix and every other app. Without a library of great content that other streamers have or social capabilities that other apps use, Quibi needed one show to get people to open the app. That never happened. There was no reason to ever open Quibi. A streaming service needs to feel essential to people’s daily lives to survive; Quibi never even made the case to get people to download. 8. If I’m on my phone, I’d rather watch TikTok Streaming services and social media apps aren’t just vying for your credit card; they also want your attention — constantly. If people are spending their days watching Netflix, playing Fortnite, scrolling through TikTok, and posting on Instagram, it’s going to require something exceptional to take their attention away. Quibi was full of spaghetti content — noodles thrown at the wall to see what sticks. While Quibi tried to get people’s attention, time spent on the aforementioned apps (and sites like Twitch and YouTube) grew rapidly. It wasn’t that people didn’t have more time at home to watch things; they just didn’t want to watch Quibi. 9. An ongoing fight over Quibi’s main technology It didn’t help that throughout all of Quibi’s short lifespan the company was facing a lawsuit from a competitive and well-financed tech company, Eko, over the app’s Turnstyle technology. That’s the very tech Quibi prided its seamless portrait / landscape mode transitions on. While the lawsuit by itself likely didn’t finish Quibi off, having to fend off a legal challenge to its key technology was just more kindling for the already growing fire. [Image: 10. Its entire thesis is wrong I can not stress this enough: Quibi didn’t work because no one at Quibi knew what it should be, what people wanted, or how people use their phones. Its entire existence is predicated on the idea that people want high-quality shortform content every single day, but executives arrogantly failed to acknowledge the simple point that people have routinely been getting that, for free, for years. Quibi didn’t fail because TikTok existed; it failed because executives refused to see TikTok as its biggest competition. Instead of learning from the very apps people spend hours on every day, Quibi stuck its nose up and said, “we’re doing something different” — even if no one is particularly interested. 11. And yes, the pandemic Fine, Katzenberg: yes, the pandemic probably hurt Quibi. It didn’t single-handedly kill Quibi, though. All of the above points — not being able to adapt, bad content, lack of social sharing, no effective marketing — weren’t because of the pandemic. It was because of poor leadership and a lack of insight into consumer behavior, wants, and needs. Did the pandemic hurt Quibi by removing the coffee lines and subway rides during which people potentially could have watched its shows? I doubt it. Even if the pandemic didn’t happen, Quibi would have failed. It just would have taken another few months. Quibi’s problems were built into Quibi’s design. The fatal blows were delivered before it even launched. The pandemic just accelerated its demise the same way the pandemic has accelerated unprecedented success for many of Quibi’s competitors that got it right.

articles.title: Quibi’s epic fall and the future of books
articles.summary: How Quibi managed to launch and close a streaming service within a year and a debate over the future of print and digital books.
articles.body: The Quibi story is both short and epic. In January 2020, company founder Jeffrey Katzenberg and CEO Meg Whitman were onstage at CES delivering an hour-long presentation on how they were about to upend the entertainment business. They’d developed new tech, signed up seemingly half the stars in Hollywood, and had raised more than a billion dollars to pull it off. By October, it was all over. Quibi was shutting down. [Video: Quibi’s epic fall and the future of books | The Vergecast] On this episode of The Vergecast, we’re once again trying out a couple of our favorite new show formats. First up is the rewatch show, which we’re calling Version History. We talk through the whole story of Quibi, from its early days as NewTV to its extremely ill-timed launch and ultimate demise. Is there a world in which Quibi could have worked? Could a company called Quibi have actually succeeded? We have much to discuss. Next, we try out our as-yet-untitled debate show, in which The Verge’s Kevin Nguyen and Alex Cranz take on a surprisingly contentious topic: is the future of books print or digital? Each gets to make their case, before having it ruthlessly ripped to shreds in front of their eyes. (We’d love to know what you think about these new formats, by the way! We’re trying out lots of new stuff, and we’re always looking to expand and even launch new shows — so we want to know everything you think we should do more of, do less of, or do differently. You can send us an email at vergecast@theverge.com, call the hotline at 866-VERGE11, or just leave us a comment here.) Finally, we answer a question from the Vergecast Hotline about a very unusual shopping situation for MP3 players. Turns out, there are good reasons to still want a dedicated music player. If you want to know more about everything we discuss in this episode, here are some links to get you started, first on Quibi: * From Variety: Quibi Has Raised $1.75B After Closing $750M Round to Fund Launch * From Variety: Jeffrey Katzenberg’s NewTV Closes $1B, Major Studios Among Investors * Quibi’s CES 2020 launch * Quibi app review: shortform streaming in a shifting landscape * Steven Spielberg is writing a horror series you’ll only be able to stream at night * Quibi’s Super Bowl 2020 commercial * Quibi versus the world * From The Wall Street Journal: Jeffrey Katzenberg and Meg Whitman Struggle With Their Startup—and Each Other * How Quibi imploded less than six months after launch * 11 reasons why Quibi crashed and burned in less than a year And on the future of books: * The Boox Palma is an amazing gadget I didn’t even know I wanted * Kobo’s great color e-readers are held back by lock-in * From The Wall Street Journal: How the Kindle Became a Must-Have Accessory (Again) And on MP3 players: * Our pick: NW-E394 Walkman Digital Music Player The Vergecast A podcast about technology and emotions Subscribe

articles.title: Logitech has created a Stream Deck for Photoshop and Premiere Pro
articles.summary: Logitech has created a creative console for Photoshop and Premiere Pro. The Stream Deck-like hardware includes a keypad and a dialpad to speed up creative tasks.
articles.body: After acquiring Stream Deck rival Loupedeck last year, Logitech is launching a $199.99 MX Creative Console that’s designed to control Adobe Photoshop and Premiere Pro. The control panel includes a Stream Deck-like keypad and a dialpad that has an analog dial and plenty of buttons to speed up creative tasks. Logitech has created custom plugins for Adobe apps like Photoshop, Lightroom Classic, Premiere Pro, After Effects, Audition, and Illustrator for its MX Creative Console. In Premiere Pro you can use the dial to scrub through a timeline, and there are four buttons around the dial to activate functions like undo. There’s also a roller for navigation, allowing you to easily adjust the level of zoom on a Premiere Pro timeline for more precise edits. In Photoshop you can twist the main dial to adjust brush sizes, or zoom in and out using the roller. [Image: The keypad and dial combo can be placed right next to your keyboard. The main keypad works much like a Stream Deck, with nine customizable LCD keys that can be used to launch apps or control different features inside apps like Photoshop or Premiere Pro. There are also two page buttons at the bottom so you can create 15 pages of keys for each app. All of the controls are fully customizable through Logitech’s app, with presets you can drag and drop onto the buttons for each app. It helps automate repetitive tasks into a single button press that usually require a few clicks or memorizing numerous keyboard shortcuts. [Image: You can customize each button and key inside Logitech’s Creative Console app. While this type of hardware combination will certainly speed up creative tasks in apps, if you already have the muscle memory of knowing a variety of keyboard shortcuts then the Creative Console might be slightly less useful. The dialpad alone could make this $199.99 device worth it for some though, thanks to the dial and roller precision tools that are unlike controlling apps using a mouse or keyboard. Logitech is launching the MX Creative Console in pale grey and graphite models, and it’s even bundling three months of Adobe’s Creative Cloud membership. The main keypad connects to a PC or Mac through USB-C, and the dialpad connects via Bluetooth or Logitech’s Bolt dongle (sold separately). The MX Creative Console enters a crowded market, going up against editing consoles like the TourBox Elite, Loupedeck Creative Tool, DaVinci Resolve editing keyboards, and even Elgato’s Stream Deck. Logitech will start shipping the MX Creative Console for $199.99 on October 14th, with preorders beginning today.

articles.title: Adobe’s AI Acrobat file hub is designed for more than PDFs
articles.summary: Acrobat Studio combines PDF tools with Adobe’s Express content creation platform and AI assistants to automate specific productivity tasks.
articles.body: Adobe is introducing a new Acrobat platform that combines the PDF app with its Adobe Express content creation service and AI assistants that can automate specific productivity tasks. Acrobat Studio allows users to upload up to 100 documents and consolidate the information together into a single workspace. The idea is to evolve Acrobat beyond being a tool just for reading and editing PDFs, into a platform that supports a wider range of file types and productivity tools, including web pages and Microsoft 365 files. The platform enables users to work on multiple documents simultaneously without leaving Acrobat, using collaborative work environments called “PDF Spaces” that pull file and website information into “conversational knowledge hubs.” These PDF spaces allow users to view and sign agreements for a project, consolidate research and notes, and use built-in Express tools to turn data into infographics or visual assets that can be shared with colleagues and clients. Acrobat Studio also includes customizable AI agents in these PDF Spaces that build on previous AI features released for Adobe’s standard Acrobat software. The AI assistants can be used by individuals and teams to offer insights, recommendations, and notes, and can generate ideas and citations from the collated data. [Image: Acrobat Studio aims to give you all the AI and design tools you might need to work on information from multiple files. Acrobat Studio is available globally in English starting today with unlimited access to PDF Spaces, AI Assistants, and Adobe Express Premium, and is offered as a separate subscription product that can replace Adobe’s Acrobat Standard and Acrobat Pro plans. Early access pricing begins at $24.99 per month for individuals and $29.99 per month for teams for an annual contract. It’s unclear what this pricing will increase to when the early-access offer expires on October 31st.

articles.title: Your smart TV may be crawling the web for AI
articles.summary: ﻿Some TV apps let you watch programming with fewer ads, as long as you allow your TV to participate in a global proxy network.
articles.body: This is Lowpass by Janko Roettgers, a newsletter on the ever-evolving intersection of tech and entertainment, syndicated just for The Verge subscribers once a week. These days, if you sign up for a new streaming service, you generally have two options: Either pay a massive premium for an ad-free experience, or endure frequent commercial breaks and all the sneaky tracking that comes with ad targeting. Web data aggregator Bright Data has been pitching streaming service operators on an alternative approach for apps running on Samsung’s Tizen and LG’s webOS platform — one that comes without ads and sky-high fees. All publishers have to do to unlock a new revenue source is integrate the company’s Bright SDK into their TV apps and convince viewers to opt into Bright’s monetization network. “We don’t do any kind of tracking,” explained Bright Data’s chief product officer, Ariel Shulman, during a webinar for streaming industry insiders two years ago. “We work silently in the background, and completely anonymously. Users don’t actually see or don’t feel anything.” The catch? With Bright’s SDK, a viewer’s smart TV becomes part of a massive global proxy network that crawls and scrapes the web. Including apps running on desktop PCs and mobile devices, the company claims to operate 150 million such residential proxies worldwide. Together, these devices gather petabytes of public web data from a wide range of different locations and IP addresses. This approach allows the company to capture localized versions of websites, but also helps to circumvent web crawler blacklists. The gathered data is then resold to companies to train AI models, among other things. Here’s how Bright’s smart TV partnerships work: When a consumer downloads and installs a participating app, they’ll see an opt-in screen asking them to confirm their willingness to participate in Bright’s proxy network. For instance, for an app called Petflix that was until recently available on the Roku app store, the note reads: “To enjoy Petflix for free with fewer ads, you are allowing Bright Data to occasionally use your device’s free resources and IP address to download public web data from the internet. Bright Data will only use your IP address for approved business-related use cases. None of your personal information is accessed or collected except your IP address. Period.” “Our network is based on consensual individual participation,” explains Bright Data spokesperson Jennifer Burns. “All users can opt-out at any time via a fast two-click process.” Once a consumer opts in to Bright Data’s network, their smart TV starts downloading publicly available webpages as well as audio and video data, which is then forwarded to Bright’s cloud servers. The company claims to only do so when it doesn’t impact the device’s bandwidth or processing capacities, with Shulman saying that individual devices download only around 50MB of data per day. In reality, there is no way for a user to know whether the SDK downloads web data at any given moment. In some cases, your smart TV may even crawl the web for Bright as soon as you turn it on. “On some operating systems, [...] our SDK is given permissions by the user to run in the background,” Shulman explained during his webinar. “This means that our monetization continues even if the app itself is not running.” All it takes for consumers is to run the app once and opt in to Bright’s network, and the device will keep crawling the web every day until they opt out again or uninstall the app. Bright Data is not the only company operating such residential proxy networks. Some of its competitors have come under fire for unsavory business practices. Last month, Google took action against the IPIDEA network, which Google’s Threat Intelligence Group called “the world’s largest proxy network.” IPIDEA worked with a number of SDK providers to distribute its code in third-party apps, including on smart TVs. Once devices were enrolled in its network, IPIDEA’s operators allegedly rented out those resources to hacking groups in China, North Korea, Iran, and Russia. “We [...] observe IPIDEA being leveraged by a vast array of espionage, crime, and information operations threat actors,” Google’s Threat Intelligence Group wrote in a January blog post. To be clear: Google’s security researchers did not draw any connection whatsoever between IPIDEA and Bright Data, and Bright goes to great lengths to set itself apart from bad actors. “Our SDK, along with all of our technology, is reviewed by Apesteem, Google, McAfee, and more, and audited regularly, most recently by PwC,” says Burns. “Bright SDK implements rigorous partner selection criteria and vets every application through strict compliance processes.” The company has nonetheless been impacted by a broader backlash against residential proxy activities. Google has adopted policies against proxy SDKs running in the background, and is now telling developers that they’re only allowed to use proxy services “in apps where that is the primary, user-facing core purpose of the app.” Amazon added a provision to its developer policies that outright bans “apps that facilitate proxy services to third parties.” Roku also bars developers from using Bright SDK and similar proxy services. All those changes have made it more difficult to figure out how widespread the use of the SDK on smart TVs actually is. A few dozen Fire TV apps still mention the SDK on Amazon’s app store, but don’t appear to make use of it anymore. I was able to download a few apps from Roku’s store that were still using the SDK, including the aforementioned Petflix app. However, those apps disappeared from the store after I contacted Roku for this story. New restrictions against proxy SDKs have had a direct impact on Bright’s addressable market in the smart TV space. The company used to pitch its solution to Roku, Android TV, and Fire TV app developers, but Burns tells me that it no longer supports these platforms. Bright does still list Samsung’s Tizen OS and LG’s webOS as supported smart TV platforms, and has published more than 200 first-party apps to LG’s app store alone. LG spokesperson Léa Lee tells me that Bright SDK is “not officially supported by LG, and their operation on the webOS platform is not guaranteed.” Samsung did not respond to multiple requests for comment. There are arguably many legitimate use cases for web crawling. “Our network serves exclusively legitimate purposes, supporting journalists, non-profits, academic researchers, cybersecurity companies, and other leading businesses worldwide,” says Burns. The problem is that consumers have no idea whether that legitimate purpose is something that aligns with their own personal values. Case in point: Bright Data does support a number of nonprofits, including some that use its proxy network to track hate speech on social media. However, the company also works with AMCHA Initiative. The group maintains an “anti-zionist faculty barometer” and includes student and faculty statements against Israel’s war in Gaza, as well as calls for schools to divest from the country, in its antisemitic incident tracker. With AI companies facing scrutiny over their environmental impact, treatment of intellectual property, and potential to replace human labor, some consumers may also feel uneasy about their TVs gathering data to train AI models. Now, some consumers may decide that such concerns are overblown, and willingly opt in to Bright’s network if it means that they get to watch fewer ads or pay less for their streaming services. I, for one, would rather watch an extra ad break or two.

articles.title: Fox wants to take over your TV — and the tech inside it
articles.summary: Fox’s $22 billion acquisition of Roku will put the media giant in charge of one of the most popular streaming device and smart TV platforms.
articles.body: Fox is about to take over the TVs in more than 100 million homes worldwide. On Monday, Fox announced that it’s acquiring Roku, the streaming middleman that serves as a portal for viewers to hop into services like Netflix, Disney Plus, Hulu, and more. The $22 billion deal may not change Roku’s familiar purple interface, but it could put Fox in control of your data behind the screen. During a call with investors, Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch said the plan is to keep the two companies separate. Fox aims to grow its business by adding Fox Sports, news content, and local stations to Roku — one of the most popular streaming device and smart TV platforms. “I would expect that we can grow our viewership in the US with a combination of Roku technology, Roku’s platform, the tremendous content that’s on the Roku channel, and the content that Fox brings to it as well,” Murdoch said. Roku founder and CEO Anthony Wood, who will have a role at the combined company after the deal closes in 2027, echoed this idea, saying that the streaming platform would feature Fox content on its homescreen, which currently shows a large marquee ad, along with a carousel filled with suggested shows and movies. “Most items on the homescreen are personalized in the sense that we decide what to show a customer based on what they’re most likely to watch, what they’re most likely to buy,” Wood told investors. “Having more properties that generate more revenue — and being able to decide when to promote them and when not to promote them — will result in overall more revenue being generated by the homescreen.” The multibillion-dollar deal may not result in an obvious branding change for Roku, but it may raise alarm bells for the people paying attention to the recent wave of media acquisitions that have put the Trump-friendly Ellison family in charge of Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount, CBS News, and, to an extent, TikTok. Lachlan Murdoch, who took the reins of Fox and its Trump-aligned news network last year, also owns The Wall Street Journal parent company News Corp. “In the Trump era, these deals have huge political implications that really need to be focused on,” Jeff Chester, the executive director of the Center for Digital Democracy, a nonprofit digital rights and consumer protection organization, tells The Verge. “Perhaps people will get the message that this is not just a media deal, this is the further political alignment of US media assets into MAGA-friendly hands.” Though Roku is known for its fleet of streaming sticks and affordable TVs, it makes most of its money by selling ads across its platform and the commission it earns when people sign up for a premium streaming service through its interface. In April, Roku offered a breakdown of how much it earns from both segments for the first time. It reported earning $613 million from advertising, while subscriptions raked in $519 million during the quarter. “Fox is getting a lot in terms of this deal, as far as distribution goes,” Dan Rayburn, a streaming media analyst, tells The Verge, adding that Fox will also gain “insight into all the data on what people are watching.” Roku offers a limited amount of original content through The Roku Channel, its free, ad-supported streaming (FAST) service, which directly competes with Fox’s own FAST service, Tubi. Despite the similarities between both services, Murdoch told investors that one-third of Tubi viewers overlap with the people watching The Roku Channel. “Bring the two of them together, [and it] effectively triples the reach of the combined service,” Murdoch said. “It’s too early to say, but our expectation is fully to keep the services separate. They serve consumers or viewers in different ways.” Roku has begun dabbling in paid subscriptions, too, with the acquisition of the $6.99-per-month Frndly streaming service, followed by the launch of Howdy, an even cheaper $2.99-per-month ad-free streaming subscription. Meanwhile, Fox recently launched its own Fox One streaming service and also has a deal with Hulu to air shows like Family Guy and The Masked Singer on the platform. With this deal, Roku could gain access to premium content to put inside its services. “I wouldn’t be surprised if Roku is now like, ‘Okay, well, now let’s go look at some content we think worked great for our platform, and we have the backing to do it,”’ Rayburn says. As we saw with Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, Fox may not see much pushback from federal regulators. “In the US … I don’t think there’ll be any regulatory review,” Rayburn says, while casting doubt on an inquiry from the European Union, where Roku and Fox have a smaller footprint. That hands-off approach from regulators could pave the way for the deal to close next year.

articles.title: The union drive at the Wikimedia Foundation is expanding
articles.summary: US-based employees say they will file for a union election with the National Labor Relations Board.
articles.body: In June, UK staff at the nonprofit that runs Wikipedia became the first to announce their intention to form a union. Now, US-based employees at the Wikimedia Foundation are joining the union drive, but management at the nonprofit has declined to voluntarily recognize their union. “While the Wikimedia Foundation touts to the public that they plan to take a neutral stance in our organizing efforts, they have already proven that not to be the case behind the scenes,” a press release sent by Communications Workers of America, with which Wiki Workers United is affiliated, reads in part. “When the Foundation rejected our request for voluntary recognition this week, they immediately sent out to employees and the public statements couched in classic union-busting rhetoric, rhetoric undoubtedly provided by outrageously expensive union-avoidance law firms. This insulting and wasteful use of Foundation resources is both an insult to Foundation employees and to the Free Knowledge Movement as a whole.” In a public statement, the foundation said it believes a secret ballot election with the NLRB is the “appropriate path forward.” The unionization efforts come at a time when tensions are high between the foundation and the thousands of unpaid volunteers who edit, write, and maintain Wikipedia. In May, hundreds of Wikipedia editors threatened to go on strike after the foundation dissolved an engineering team that worked closely with volunteers. Some volunteers questioned whether the layoffs were related to union efforts, which the foundation denied.

articles.title: Twitch streamers can now opt out from training Amazon’s AI
articles.summary: Twitch users can now opt out of allowing their streams and other content to be used to train Amazon’s generative AI models. The toggle is available in settings.
articles.body: Twitch users can now opt out of allowing their content to be used to train Amazon’s generative AI models. Opting out means that “your streams, VODs, clips, stream chats, and pictures and text on your channel” won’t be used in “future training” of an Amazon AI model “whose purpose is to generate or synthesize text, audio, images, or video,” according to a Twitch support page. Other “AI-supported” features like captions and safety tools will still function if you opt out of generative AI training. However, if you participate in a chat on another person’s stream, “their opt-out preferences govern if that chat can be used for training,” Twitch says. The “Training for Generative AI” toggle is present for me in Twitch’s settings under the Security and Privacy tab. It was toggled on when I found it, and I’ve asked Amazon if that’s the default. Here’s the full text of Amazon’s description for the toggle: > Allow your channel content to train generative AI content models at Amazon. Turning this off does not opt you out of Twitch and Amazon using your channel content for other purposes described in the Twitch Privacy Notice, including using AI-supported Twitch features that benefit the community by facilitating streamer growth and monetization (such as real-time sponsorship campaign assistance), viewer discovery (such as recommendations), and community safety (such as AutoMod). articles.title: Twitch Now Trains Amazon's Generative AI Models on Your Channel by Default
articles.summary: Twitch has rolled out a new "feature" that trains Amazon's generative AI content models on its users' channels. The setting can be disabled, but it's turned on by default.
articles.body:
Twitch has rolled out a new "feature" that trains Amazon's generative AI content models on its users' channels. The setting can be disabled, but it's turned on by default.

"Allow your channel content to train generative AI content models at Amazon," reads the setting, which is buried in your user settings and is enabled by default.

To disable the setting, navigate to the Security and Privacy tab of your Twitch user settings and uncheck the "Training for Generative AI" toggle. This will disable Twitch from using your channel content to train Amazon's AI models on that content, but does not opt you out of Amazon using your channel content for other uses, per the Twitch Privacy Notice .

While it's easy enough to disable, having this setting turned on by default is a slap in the face for users who don't want anything to do with generative AI. Notably, the top post on the Feature Requests section of Twitch's User Voice forums is an ask to make all AI features optional and opted out of by default. That post has more than 13,000 votes and 4,000 comments in support, compared to around 250 votes for the next three highest-voted suggestions.

In a stream (on Twitch, of course) discussing the new setting , Twitch Chief Product Officer Mike Minton responded to criticism by saying the quiet part out loud. "If it was opt-in, nobody would opt in," Minton said. "So it's going to be on by default."

This comes as generative AI features (and the slop they churn out) seem to be worming their way into every aspect of our digital lives. Things have gotten so bad that Linkedin recently rolled out a feature to report content that carries the stink of AI slop .

Meanwhile, the datacenter infrastructure buildout to support and run these AI tools is the primary cause of the ongoing RAM crisis that has driven up the price of gaming hardware . AI is a bad deal for gamers that we didn't ask for – if we did, companies wouldn't have to make their sloppy "features" enabled by default.

Bo Moore is IGN's Senior Manager of Tech. You can find him online @usebomswisely.

articles.title: Ocasio-Cortez calls focus on Hasan Piker 'absolutely ludicrous' as some Democrats demand distance
articles.summary: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez called it "ludicrous" that Congress is focused on Twitch streamer Hasan Piker as Democrats debate his political influence.
articles.body: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., brushed off far-left streamer Hasan Piker's role in American politics on Thursday, questioning why people were focused or devoting time to him. "It is absolutely ludicrous that so much oxygen from sitting elected officials in the United States Congress is being dedicated to discourse around a Twitch streamer for young people," Ocasio-Cortez, a member of the progressive Squad, said according to The Hill. Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., also didn't dismiss him outright, telling the outlet she wouldn't defend all his views. MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT DEMANDS REPORTERS STOP ASKING 'ABOUT HASAN PIKER' AHEAD OF SENATE RACE "That's for him to do," Jayapal said. "I don’t know why, all of a sudden, the standard is you have to agree with everything he said." HASAN PIKER IS BECOMING THE 'FACE OF THE PROGRESSIVE MOVEMENT,' FORMER DEMOCRATIC OPERATIVE WARNS Jaypal told the outlet Democrats needed to reach Piker's voters. "I think that we have been talking about how we need to reach out to all parts of our party and also how difficult it is sometimes to get people to pay attention to politics, and, so, streamers are important in that," Jayapal said. The Hill cited multiple Democrats who have dismissed Piker, including Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., who told the outlet, "Not only should people not be on stage with him or take his support, they should condemn his views and what he has said. "And I think anything short of that is unacceptable." SOME DEMOCRATS PRIVATELY DISGUSTED BY HASAN PIKER BUT ARE AFRAID TO PUBLICLY CRITICIZE HIM, HOUSE DEM CLAIMS Piker has campaigned with several Democrats this midterm election cycle, including Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for Senate in Michigan. Other Democrats have expressed the importance of reaching Piker's listeners, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. Sanders was asked about Piker's past statements on 9/11, which the streamer has since walked back. Sanders condemned the comments and told CNN in August, "He has a whole lot of followers and a lot of things that he's saying that are making sense to a lot of people. I think, you know, we have to get above cancel culture. You know, when you're doing radio, whatever they do, podcasts three hours a day, you say dumb things." ABDUL EL-SAYED PLAYS DOWN HASAN PIKER TIES AFTER STREAMER’S VIRAL ANTISEMITISM FIRESTORM Speaking to Stephen A. Smith during his show, "Straight Shooter," El-Sayed said this week he was trying to reach Piker's listeners. "What I'm saying is there are 3 million people who listen to Hasan," El-Sayed said. "I want to offer them a pathway into an electoral movement where, rather than sit outside of the electoral system, they see a pathway around the things that they agree with that he says that I agree with and a pathway that disavows the things that I disagree with. And, so, it's important." Smith summarized El-Sayed's strategy as an effort to win over Piker's audience rather than an endorsement of the streamer personally. "So, you're not thinking about him. You’re not thinking about him. You’re thinking about the 3 million people that support him, and you're trying to get those votes. That's what you're saying?" Smith said. DEM CANDIDATE ERUPTS IN PROFANE DEFENSE OF HASAN PIKER AS PARTY FIGURES DISTANCE THEMSELVES "Exactly," El-Sayed said. Fox News Digital reported last week that El-Sayed attempted to put distance between his campaign and Piker after the streamer faced backlash over comments about American Jews and Israel. Piker endorsed El-Sayed and appeared at multiple campaign events, including his primary night gathering. Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital in a statement, "A lot of these folks are being rather disingenuous. Yes, media is running wild, arguably disproportionately so, with this Piker story, but a big reason for that is El-Sayed’s hard to understand refusal to create more distance between himself and the streamer or just flat disavow him. "You can’t have it both ways. Either he is just some random streamer or he is a critical figure for the left’s political movement. His refusal to … denounce him suggests the latter, though strategically it seems Piker is more of a liability than a help. Recent polling showed the vast majority of Democrats don’t like him." Schroff said Democrats like him have been consistent in calling out President Donald Trump for "dining with Nick Fuentes and bringing Laura Loomer into his inner circle." "And the reason certain candidates do have the burden to disavow Piker is not because he is some influencer who boosts them. … They have actively sought him out, campaigned with him and joined his streaming platform," he added. "Normal Democrats do not want to be associated with the insane things Piker has said." "AOC, Bernie Sanders and Abdul El-Sayed rolled out the red carpet for Hasan Piker, but now that voters are catching on to how insane his views are, they've developed a sudden case of amnesia," RNC spokesman Max Lippel told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Piker has always been an America-hating extremist, and if they didn't want to answer for his disgusting views, they should have never requested he campaign with them to begin with." articles.title: Outnumbered: The IAF pilot who took on four Pakistani Sabres and helped save Calcutta
articles.summary: News News: The morning of September 7, 1965, brought one of the more remarkable air battles of the war to the skies over Kalaikunda, and at its heart was Flight .
articles.body: The morning of September 7, 1965, brought one of the more remarkable air battles of the war to the skies over Kalaikunda, and at its heart was Flight Lieutenant Alfred Cooke, whose outnumbered Hunter took on four Pakistani Sabres and lived to tell an extraordinary tale. It came just hours after Kalaikunda had already been mauled once that morning, when five Sabres led by Squadron Leader Shabbir Syed struck the airbase, catching it completely off guard and destroying two Canberra bombers along with four Vampires on the ground.Buoyed by that success of this air raid, the Pakistan Air Force made the same mistake the IAF had made earlier over Sargodha, sending in a second raid against a target that was now fully alert. At around 10:30 am, radar officer Squadron Leader "Mama" Sahni picked up a fleeting blip near Port Canning and immediately alerted Kalaikunda air base. Two Hunters flying Combat Air Patrol some 60 miles north of the base, piloted by Flight Lieutenant Alfred Cooke and Flying Officer SC Mamgain, both of 14 Squadron (which now flies Jaguars), were asked to return to defend the base and arrived over Kalaikunda at 4,000 feet, at the altitude needed to intercept the four incoming low flying Sabres led by Flight Lieutenant Haleem of the 14 Squadron of the PAF.What followed was a chaotic, low-level dogfight witnessed by cheering students of IIT Kharagpur watching from their rooftops. On spotting the Hunters, the Sabres split, two engaging Cooke head-on while the other pair peeled off toward the airfield. Cooke later admitted he remembered little beyond Sabres seemingly everywhere, but his gun camera film tells a remarkable story, he fired on four different Sabres and hit three of them. The first broke up in mid-air, killing Flight Lieutenant Afzal Khan. Cooke damaged a second and third Sabre, then latched onto a fourth, chasing it relentlessly through low-level breaks and turns until he ran out of ammunition, yet stayed on its tail anyway, rattling the Pakistani pilot enough to force him off his attack run and all the way back to the border.Those watching from the ground, reported seeing two Sabres go down, a claim partly corroborated by police reports of a smoking jet and a pilot ejecting near the border. Pakistan admitted losing one Sabre, flown by Flight Lieutenant Tariq Habib, that limped back too damaged to salvage, matching the aircraft visible in Cooke's own gun camera footage. Despite the PAF's gamble to press its advantage, Kalaikunda stayed operational for the rest of the war.

Instead, Lynch chased off the wrong stable member, which ultimately allowed for Morgan to capitalize.Tonight was only the second defense of Morgan's dreadful title reign since April, when she first won the strap. Everything Judgment Day needs to end or be drastically refreshed as soon as possible.There is NO love lost between @YaOnlyLivvOnce and @BeckyLynchWWE 😬 pic.twitter.com/6LaX7gs7FI— WWE (@WWE) September 8, 2026 A Full VisionThe Vision has never been fuller with its current five-person lineup of Bron Breakker, Bronson Reed, Logan Paul, Austin Theory and Maxxine Dupri. articles.title: College football scores, results: SMU holds off Florida State to win on late FG after long delay at start of game
articles.summary: Week 1 wrapped up with SMU pulling out a narrow win over Florida State.
articles.body: Week 1 wrapped up Monday with an ACC showdown in Tallahassee that didn't disappoint despite a late start as No. 19 SMU held off Florida State for a 27-24 win.The game was delayed more than 90 minutes due to a power outage. Per ESPN's broadcast, a transformer blew as the power was trying to be restored to the stadium. What was set to be a very brief delay stretched out well over an hour as players from both teams went back to their locker rooms.But when they were finally on the field, it was a show — albeit one that featured a lot of head-scratching mistakes. The Mustangs constantly kicked themselves in the foot and gave the Seminoles several chances to stay in the game despite an offense that was nearly unstoppable with Kevin Jennings at the helm. The star QB threw for a career-high 430 yards and three touchdowns — but also accounted for two of SMU's four turnovers.The Mustangs were one of the favorites in the ACC and are capable of getting back to the playoff for the second time in three seasons with a healthy Jennings, but they have plenty to clean up after Monday's win.For Florida State, the result is a bitter pill. The Seminoles were in the game late despite a stunning lack of defense and not much output from Ashton Daniels and its offense. It'll put even more pressure on FSU coach Mike Norvell, who was roundly booed for his decision-making and when he was shown on the video board to the home crowd at Doak Campbell Stadium. articles.title: How to stream safely while traveling outside the US
articles.summary: A VPN encrypts your connection on hotel, airport and café Wi-Fi abroad, but streaming catalogs and live sports access still depend on provider rules.
articles.body: Traveling abroad used to mean leaving your normal entertainment routine at home. Now, your streaming subscriptions can come with you. However, hotels, airports and cafés often mean unfamiliar Wi-Fi networks and different streaming catalogs. If you want to stream safely while traveling outside the U.S., a VPN, or virtual private network, can help. It creates an encrypted connection between your device and the VPN server. That adds useful protection when you are on a network you do not control. A VPN can also let you choose a server in your home country. That can be useful when you sign in to streaming services you already use. Still, content availability depends on the service, your subscription and local licensing rules. Here's what to know before you travel so you can protect your connection, stream more smoothly and avoid surprises along the way. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com INSTANTLY UPGRADE YOUR STREAMING: AT HOME AND WHEN TRAVELING Why public Wi-Fi deserves extra caution Free Wi-Fi makes travel easier. Yet you often do not know who runs the network, how it is configured or who else is connected. Most major websites and apps already use HTTPS encryption. Even so, a VPN adds another encrypted tunnel between your device and the VPN server. That can reduce what the local network can learn about your internet activity. This protection is useful beyond streaming. You may check email, book a reservation or sign in to an account while you are away. Turning on a VPN before using unfamiliar Wi-Fi adds another layer of privacy. Of course, a VPN does not make every public network risk-free. You should still avoid suspicious Wi-Fi names, keep your devices updated and use strong account security. Keeping up with your usual streaming services abroad Streaming can get more complicated when you cross international borders. A service may offer one catalog in the U.S. and another in Europe or Australia. Licensing agreements, regional rights and company policies often determine what appears. A VPN can be useful here because it gives you a secure way to connect to the internet while you sign in to subscriptions you normally use at home. You can also choose a VPN server in the U.S. when you need a U.S.-based connection. However, a VPN does not guarantee access to a particular show, movie, channel or sporting event. Streaming companies set their own terms of use and regional availability rules. A program you watch at home may therefore be unavailable at your destination. Before you travel, check your streaming provider's current policies and the availability of anything you especially want to watch. Watch U.S. TV online in 3 easy steps If you want a secure U.S. connection while traveling, set everything up before you leave. That way, you are not troubleshooting from an airport lounge or hotel room. Step 1: Sign up for a VPN Choose a reputable VPN service and create your account before your trip. Look for one that offers U.S. server locations, apps for the devices you use and enough simultaneous connections for the people traveling with you. Step 2: Download the latest VPN app Install the VPN app on every phone, tablet or computer you plan to bring. Then, sign in and test the connection before you leave home. This also gives you time to solve any password, installation or account problems while you still have a reliable connection. Step 3: Connect to a VPN server in the U.S. Open your VPN and choose a U.S. server location. Once connected, open your streaming service and sign in normally. Websites and streaming services see the VPN server's IP address instead of your usual public IP address, while the connection between your device and the VPN server remains encrypted. Your streaming provider still decides what programming your account can access. TRAVEL MISTAKE PUTS PHONE, LAPTOP AND STREAMING ACCOUNTS AT RISK What U.S. TV can you watch with a VPN? Streaming services have their own rules for VPN connections, regional access and travel. Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, Amazon Prime Video, YouTube, ESPN and Apple TV+ may handle VPN connections differently, so check your service before you travel. The exact shows, movies, channels and sporting events you can watch also depend on your subscription and the streaming provider's regional rules. That is especially important for live TV and sports. Broadcast rights can change by country, league and even individual event. If there is something specific you want to watch during your trip, check the service before you leave. Streaming U.S. sports while you travel A VPN can also protect your connection while you watch live sports through subscriptions you already have. That can be useful for football, basketball, baseball, hockey, tennis, cycling, golf and other events when you are away from home. However, a VPN does not create a subscription or eliminate a provider's blackout rules. Your streaming service still controls access based on your plan, location and its current broadcasting agreements. For that reason, check the event and service before relying on it for a big game. Set everything up before you leave The best time to prepare is before you are standing in an airport with spotty Wi-Fi. Download the VPN app on your phone, tablet or laptop. Sign in and test it. Also, update your streaming apps before departure. Next, sign in to the services you expect to use. Some platforms may ask you to verify your identity when they detect a new device or location. Handling that at home can save time later. If your service supports offline viewing, download a few shows or movies before you go. Offline downloads are especially useful on planes, trains and trips where the connection may be unreliable. Choosing a VPN server for streaming When you use a VPN, your traffic travels through the VPN server before reaching the internet. Distance can affect performance. If you mainly want extra privacy and do not need a particular country, choose a nearby server. A shorter distance can often improve speed and latency. If you need a U.S. IP address for a service you normally use at home, connect to a U.S. server instead. If the stream slows down, try another server in the same country. A different location may have less congestion or better performance. What to do if your stream is buffering Not every streaming problem comes from the VPN. Hotel and airport networks can slow down when many people share the same connection. First, check the underlying Wi-Fi. Then, reconnect to the VPN or try another server. Closing apps that are downloading files, backing up photos or running large updates can also help. If the connection still struggles, lower the video quality. HD and 4K video require much more bandwidth than standard-definition video. A trusted mobile connection may also perform better than crowded public Wi-Fi, depending on your roaming plan and signal strength. THE TRICK TO SMOOTHER STREAMING AT HOME AND ON THE ROAD Streaming on Apple TV, Fire TV and Roku Traveling with a streaming device can make a hotel room feel more like home. However, VPN setup varies depending on the device. Apple TV: Some VPN providers offer dedicated Apple TV apps that you can install directly on supported models. Amazon Fire TV and Fire Stick: Many major VPN services offer apps for compatible Fire TV devices. Roku: Roku does not support traditional VPN apps directly. Instead, you generally need to connect it through a VPN-enabled router or another supported network setup. Before packing a streaming stick, check whether your hotel television gives you access to an HDMI port. Also, remember that some hotel networks use a browser-based login page. That can make connecting a streaming device more complicated. Why streaming catalogs change when you travel? A streaming service may license a movie in the U.S. but not in France, Australia or another country. Another broadcaster or streaming company may hold the rights there. As a result, the same account can show a different catalog after you cross a border. Live sports can be even more complicated because broadcasting rights often vary by market. That is why it helps to check availability before a trip. A VPN can protect your connection and change the location of the VPN server you connect through. However, it cannot change the licensing agreements behind a streaming service. Which VPN should you choose for travel? With so many VPN services available, I would focus on a few practical things. Look for strong encryption, an easy-to-use app, plenty of server locations and support for the devices you plan to bring. If you expect to stream while traveling, also check whether the VPN works well with the streaming services you use and offers servers in the countries you may need. A VPN encrypts the traffic between your device and the VPN provider's servers, which can add an important layer of privacy when you are using hotel, airport or café Wi-Fi. Before choosing one, check that it supports your phone, computer, tablet and any streaming devices you plan to use. You should also compare how many devices can connect at the same time, especially if you are traveling with family. I would also look closely at the provider's privacy practices, reputation and independent security audits. Free VPNs can come with limitations such as slower speeds, fewer server choices or questionable data practices, so read the privacy policy before installing one. Remember that a VPN is a privacy and security tool. You remain responsible for following the terms of your streaming provider and any applicable laws. For the best VPN software, see my expert review of the best VPNs for browsing the web privately on your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com/VPN. Kurt's key takeaways Streaming abroad is much easier than it used to be. Still, I would not wait until you land to figure out your setup. Install your VPN and update your streaming apps before leaving home. Sign in ahead of time, too. Then download something for offline viewing so you have a backup when hotel Wi-Fi becomes unreliable. I also like using a VPN on unfamiliar networks because streaming is only part of what we do online while traveling. You may use the same connection for email, travel reservations and other accounts. Finally, remember what a VPN can and cannot do. It can encrypt your connection and let you select the location of the VPN server you use. It cannot promise that every show, channel or game will be available everywhere you travel. articles.title: Streamer colombiano sufre intento de robo mientras transmitía en directo en plena calle de Cali
articles.standfirst: El influencer la Piquiña puso un setup para hacer un en vivo en la calle y su seguridad frustró el robo
articles.summary: El influencer la Piquiña puso un setup para hacer un en vivo en la calle y su seguridad frustró el robo
articles.body: El streamer colombiano conocido como La Piquiña vivió momentos de tensión mientras realizaba una transmisión en vivo en una calle de Cali. El hecho, que quedó registrado en video y circuló ampliamente en redes sociales, terminó sin que el creador de contenido perdiera sus equipos ni resultara herido. La situación volvió a poner sobre la mesa los riesgos a los que se exponen influencers y streamers que llevan sus producciones a espacios abiertos, especialmente cuando utilizan computadores, monitores, cámaras, iluminación y otros elementos visibles que pueden atraer la atención de delincuentes. Según las publicaciones que difundieron el caso, La Piquiña había instalado un montaje de transmisión en plena vía pública, con equipos tecnológicos y luces, para realizar contenido en directo junto a su audiencia. En medio de la emisión, un sujeto habría intentado aprovechar la exposición de los aparatos para llevárselos. Sin embargo, el sistema de seguridad dispuesto en el lugar habría impedido que el presunto ladrón concretara el hurto. El reporte difundido en redes señala que el candado de seguridad fue determinante: al no poder desprender el equipo, el hombre perdió el equilibrio y cayó al suelo. Esa reacción frustró la acción antes de que pudiera escapar con algún objeto. El caso adquirió notoriedad porque ocurrió frente a las cámaras, mientras La Piquiña estaba conectado con sus seguidores. La transmisión convirtió un momento de entretenimiento en una escena de incertidumbre, al evidenciar lo vulnerable que puede ser un creador cuando instala equipos costosos en un entorno abierto. La principal razón por la que el presunto delincuente no logró ejecutar el robo fue la protección física de los equipos. El equipo de seguridad habría impedido que pudiera retirar rápidamente los elementos utilizados en el “setup” de transmisión. La reacción de quienes acompañaban la transmisión también habría contribuido a que la situación no escalara. De acuerdo con versiones compartidas en redes, un reportero presente en la escena logró retener al sujeto después de la caída. Más allá de la viralidad del video, el caso refleja cómo la creación de contenido en exteriores puede mezclarse con problemas cotidianos de seguridad urbana. El montaje de La Piquiña, pensado para interactuar con sus seguidores, terminó atrayendo una situación de riesgo que pudo haber terminado en pérdidas económicas o una agresión. El streamer pudo continuar sin que se reportaran daños físicos ni robo de sus pertenencias, pero el episodio deja una advertencia: la exposición digital no solo ocurre en las redes. Cuando la transmisión se hace en la calle, la seguridad debe ser parte central de la producción.

articles.title: Amazon Prime Video’s new AI tech matches lips to dubbed audio
articles.summary: Amazon’s Prime Video is launching a new AI lip-syncing feature that lines up an actor’s mouth with translated speech.
articles.body: Amazon’s Prime Video is launching a new AI-powered feature that lines up an actor’s mouth with “human-dubbed” audio. The feature is only available with the English dub of the German series Maxton Hall for now, but Prime Video plans to expand it to “additional titles” in the future. In its announcement, Prime Video says it uses a combination of AI and visual effects technologies to make lip movements match up with translated speech. Meta and YouTube recently launched an AI-powered auto-dubbing feature for creators, while allowing them to turn on a “lip sync” option to make it look like creators are actually speaking in a user’s preferred language. Last year, Prime Video began experimenting with “AI-aided” dubbing in English and Spanish across 12 movies and TV shows, including El Cid: La Leyenda, Mi Mamá Lora, and Long Lost. The streamer’s lip-sync dubbing is currently available for seasons 1 and 2 of Maxton Hall for subscribers around the globe, and will launch with the show’s third season coming December 9th.

articles.title: Team USA rolls into semifinals with dominant 52-point win over Hungary, led by Napheesa Collier's 19 points
articles.summary: Team USA faces off against Hungary in the FIBA World Cup quarterfinals.
articles.body: Team USA is rolling into the FIBA World Cup semifinals after a 52-point win over Hungary in the quarterfinals on Thursday, on the back of yet another balanced attack that saw every player score.After some questions arose in the group stage following a near-upset by Italy, Team USA has largely put any concerns to bed with its last two performances, topped by a 108-56 win to advance to the semifinals. After shooting just 29% from the 3-point line in the group stage, Team USA improved that figure to 52% in this matchup, and owned nearly every other facet of the game: 52 points in the paint to Hungary's 16; 28-3 in fast break points; and 31 assists, the most ever in a FIBA World Cup quarterfinal game.USA’s ball movement 😮‍💨#FIBAWWC | @FIBAWWC pic.twitter.com/7unqof7HQV— TNT Sports U.S. (@TNTSportsUS) September 10, 2026 USA was led early and often by Player of the Game Napheesa Collier, who had a game-high 19 points, with four others scoring in double digits — Rhyne Howard posted 15, while Kahleah Copper, Caitlin Clark and Jackie Young all had 10 apiece. Clark had a game-high nine assists, several of which led to Angel Reese (9 points, 6 rebounds, 3 assists) buckets.After the game, Reese was asked about her connection with Clark, which was on full display throughout Thursday's win."We just continue to build chemistry because we know we're going to be USA teammates for a while," she told TNT's Allie LaForce after the game.For Hungary, Reka Lelik led the team with 12 points, followed by Agnes Torok's 11. Dorka Juhasz, Collier's Lynx teammate, posted a team-high eight assists.Team USA will play the winner of Thursday's Australia-Spain matchup in the semifinals on Saturday. articles.title: Have you paid for all the services you need for the NFL yet?
articles.summary: NFL streaming costs could total roughly $800 this season across Netflix, Amazon Prime, YouTube TV and more, squeezing working-class families.
articles.body: Do you have all the services required to watch the NFL this season? If not, here is a breakdown of the platforms you need and what they will cost. Thursday night’s Rams-49ers matchup in Australia will air exclusively on Netflix. The streaming service will carry five matchups this season, including games on Thanksgiving Eve, Christmas Day and in Week 18. Because of Netflix’s schedule, NFL fans will need subscriptions in September, November, December and January — four of the season’s five months. Netflix will not carry a game in October. A monthly Netflix subscription costs between $8.99 and $26.99, depending on the plan. Fans will again need Amazon Prime for five months, from Week 2 through the Wild Card Round, at $14.99 per month. YOUTUBE TV IS ABOUT TO CHANGE THE WAY WE WATCH LIVE SPORTS Those with standard cable or satellite packages will continue to receive weekly games on Fox, CBS, NBC and ESPN/ABC. However, depending on the other content they consume, fans may have more economical alternatives. YouTube now offers a $64.99-per-month Sports Plan that includes local channels, ESPN, TNT, TBS, FS1, Big Ten Network, SEC Network and more. articles.title: ‘Special 26’ in Mumbai: Sacked driver teams up with I-T officials to target ex-employer in fake raid
articles.summary: MUMBAI: In a Akshay Kumar-starrer  Special 26-style plot, a sacked driver allegedly teamed up with two Income Tax officials and others to conduct a fa.
articles.body: MUMBAI: In a Akshay Kumar-starrer Special 26-style plot, a sacked driver allegedly teamed up with two Income Tax officials and others to conduct a fake raid at his former employer’s office in Mumbai and demand Rs 1 crore. The extortion bid was foiled after the company owner asked the alleged raiding team to produce authorisation documents.Andheri police have arrested 10 people in connection with the July 17 incident, including two serving I-T officials. Police said the operation was masterminded by former company driver Santosh Khopatkar, 37, who was sacked about three months before the alleged raid and wanted revenge against his former employer.The fake raid was conducted at Two M Ophthotronics Pvt Ltd in Sahar Cargo Estate, Chakala. Police registered an FIR on September 4 following a complaint by company owner Rajkumar Kandasami.Kandasami told police that his employees called him saying I-T officials had raided the office. Two men in plain clothes later approached Kandasami and his wife near their home, introduced themselves as I-T officials and displayed an identity card. They allegedly forced the couple into an aggregator cab and took them to the office.Sub-inspector Rohan Surve said the accused questioned employees, examined company documents and took away the mobile phones of Kandasami, his wife and staff. They allegedly produced a purported search warrant and obtained Kandasami’s signature on it.The group questioned Kandasami about cash transactions, threatened him with a substantial penalty and offered to settle the purported tax case for Rs 1 crore. However, Kandasami asked them to produce authorisation documents for the raid. The alleged raiding team could not produce any and left empty-handed after around three hours.Kandasami subsequently checked with his chartered accountant and found that the Income Tax department had not ordered any raid at his company.Police said their investigation revealed that Khopatkar had provided the tip-off about the company. He had allegedly approached the I-T officials for help in raiding his former employer after being sacked.The two I-T officials arrested in the case are inspector Sureshkumar Mishra, 57, posted at the Piramal Chamber office in Lalbaug, and tax assistant Sunil Gore, 59, posted at the Kautilya Bhavan office in BKC.Police said Mishra and Gore had allegedly conducted a similar raid on a company in Manpada and demanded Rs 65 lakh.Those arrested earlier in the Chakala case include Khopatkar, Vinay More, 37, Prem Sabnani, 50, Pragnya M, Reshma Shyamrao Warang, 41, and Shabina Shaikh, 48.DCP (West Zone-3) Datta Nalawade said police also took custody of Jitendra More of Thane and Ashok Shinde of Vile Parle West on Thursday. The two were already in judicial custody in connection with the Manpada case.A team led by senior inspector Umesh Machindar, inspector Atul Nikam, assistant inspector Ramdas Kadam and sub-inspectors Rohan Surve and Rameshwar Karpe analysed call records, mobile numbers, dump data, location details and CCTV footage from government and private cameras.Investigators are examining the seized phones for calls, chats, WhatsApp messages and financial transactions to establish the alleged conspiracy, identify other associates and determine the role of each accused.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news.
